## One raised note, aimed at the next chord

A dominant chord makes a particular future likely: its own tonic, a fifth below.
A *secondary dominant* points that same expectation at some chord other than the
home tonic. For one bar, an ordinary diatonic chord gets treated like a tonic,
and the music carries on without ever leaving its key.

In C major, G is the dominant, and the dominant of G is D major. That D major
contains F-sharp, which lives outside the C-major scale and wants to rise a
semitone to G when you voice the chords so it can. The label for it is V/V,
which reads "dominant of the dominant." The slash names the chord being
approached. By itself, the slash claims nothing about the key having changed.

Controlled comparison, then. Put D minor, the plain diatonic ii, in front of G.
Then raise its F to F-sharp, turning it into D major, and leave rhythm, voicing
and synth exactly where they were. One pitch is the entire difference between
the two passes.

## D minor and D major, side by side

Both progressions run four chords and land on the same C. Roots and qualities
stay visible as data, so you can read the chromatic intervention as easily as
you can hear it. Only one pitch differs between the two passes. Will you hear
the difference at the D chord, or at the G that follows it?

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

diatonic = [
  {root: :c3, quality: :major},
  {root: :d3, quality: :minor},
  {root: :g2, quality: :major},
  {root: :c3, quality: :major}
]

tonicised = [
  {root: :c3, quality: :major},
  {root: :d3, quality: :major}, # V/V: F-sharp points toward G
  {root: :g2, quality: :major},
  {root: :c3, quality: :major}
]

define :play_progression do |chords|
  chords.each do |item|
    play_chord chord(item[:root], item[:quality]),
      release: 1.8,
      amp: 0.75
    sleep 2
  end
end

play_progression diatonic
sleep 2
play_progression tonicised
```

D minor gets you to G diatonically. D major gets you to G by declaring, in the
chord data itself, that G is the target. Listen for whether the second arrival
feels more prepared than the first.

One honest limitation before you draw conclusions. These chords are all in root
position, so F-sharp never sits directly below a higher G in a single voice.
What you're hearing is harmonic preparation, not the semitone resolution itself.
You'll build that resolution by hand in the exercise.

## Redirect the pull

1. Change the target G major to G minor in both arrays. D major still points at
   a root a fifth below it, and the B-flat that arrives recolours the whole
   destination. Listen for what survives the change and what doesn't.
2. Restore G major and make the D chord `:dom7`. The added C forms a tritone
   with F-sharp, which gives you a second tendency tone pulling in the opposite
   direction. Compare that urgency against the plainer triad.
3. Move D major away from G, so that D minor comes between them. Same chromatic
   pitches, arrival delayed. A chord that sounded directed starts to sound
   unexplained the moment its context stops answering it.

## Reading V/V as a nested address

Your home key hands you a family of diatonic chords. A secondary dominant
borrows the dominant-to-tonic relation and applies it locally to one member of
that family. Pick the target root, go a perfect fifth above it, build a major
triad or a dominant seventh. Since you built the new chord relative to the
target and not to the home scale, it usually brings at least one chromatic pitch
with it.

Slash notation works like a nested lookup. V/V resolves the right-hand V first,
finding the temporary target, then asks for V in relation to that. Your code can
resolve it in exactly those two stages: locate the target root in the current
key, move seven semitones above it, build the quality that creates the pull.

When the emphasis stays local, the word for it is *tonicisation*: the target
gets brightly prepared, and the chords after it go on supporting the home tonic.
A *modulation* lasts long enough for your ear to adopt the new tonic and
reinterpret everything around it. An outside pitch can't tell you which of the
two you've got. What comes next, and for how long, is the evidence that decides
it. [Lesson 53](53-modulation-state-change.qmd) takes that question up directly.

Voice leading is what makes the theory audible. In C major, F-sharp rises to G
while the other D-major notes find nearby positions in the G chord. Bury that
F-sharp in a distant octave, or send it downward, and the V/V is still written
on the page with its clearest melodic cue switched off.

## Tonicise a chord of your own

Write an eight-bar diatonic progression in a major key. Choose one diatonic
chord other than I and put that chord's own dominant in front of it. Keep the
original and tonicised versions in parallel data arrays and render them one
after the other with the same rhythm, voicing and synth.

Then voice the secondary dominant and its target as explicit note lists, close
enough together that the chromatic pitch resolves by step in a single voice. In
C major approaching G, that means F-sharp3 rising to G3 while no other voice
moves more than two semitones. Label the temporary target, the slash numeral and
every chromatic pitch. Leave enough unchanged harmony after the arrival to prove
the original key still governs the passage.
